Although still considerably higher than a decade ago the residual pre-tax cash-flow in $/lb terms generated during 2012 is estimated to less than half that generated in the preceding two years. - With shareholders of mining companies demanding dividend payments from residual cashflow, funds for exploration and project development may be restricted. - 2012 first year in recent times that revenues from copper and by-product metals fell, but costs rose. - Main contributors to operating cost rises in 2012 were general inflation in producing countries, increases in costs of fuel and electricity and operational issues at specific mines. projects Demand for mine production capability (refined metal) Source Wood Mackenzie © Wood Mackenzie 7 **Delivering commercial insight** **www.woodmac.com** # **Supply gap opens up again from 2017 unless new projects are developed** - Growth in refined consumption in 2012 19.8Mt compared to 19.7Mt in 2011. Demand for mine output (after accounting for scrap usage) actually fell slightly to 15.8kt pushing market for mined copper into 0.5Mt surplus. - Initial signs from China indicate improvement in end use market sectors. Pace and scale of recovery to be determined. - 3.6% p.a. average growth in refined consumption forecast over next decade. - Improved performance from existing mines and incremental capacity from new projects forecast to keep market for mined copper in surplus until 2017. - Stocks of refined metal will rise above 65 day LT average during this period. Previously support level for copper price in these circumstances has been 90th centile of C1 cost curve which will be around $2.30/lb (2012$) over the next few years. We do not expect copper price to go this low, but there will be downward pressure on copper price from a fundamental perspective. - Prices below $3.00/lb may represent a buying opportunity for the Chinese and could force closure of high cost informal Chinese producers not included in cost curve. Project cancellations due to low metal price may trigger price rises due to market sentiment. - After 2017 increased demand and reserve depletion causes supply gap to re-open unless new projects are developed. New production capability (i.e. before disruptions) by 2022 = 6.3Mt. © Wood Mackenzie 8 **Delivering commercial insight** **www.woodmac.com** # **How much can brownfield projects supply?** ## **Demand for mined copper from new greenfield projects** 28

Radomiro Tomic, El Abra, Zaldivar etc). - 70% of forecast production from brownfield projects in our probable category a good proxy based on historical precedent. Contributes 1.8Mt/a by 2022 leaving 4.5Mt/a to come from other sources. © Wood Mackenzie 10 **Delivering commercial insight** **www.woodmac.com** # **A LT copper price of $3.50/lb should incentivise sufficient new mine projects?** Project Incentive Price (PIP) Curve

### **Cumulative Production (Paid kt Cu)** Source: Wood Mackenzie © Wood Mackenzie 11 **Delivering commercial insight** **www.woodmac.com** # **A LT copper price of $3.50/lb should incentivise sufficient new mine projects?** - Our approach for forecasting LT metal price is to consider what level is required to incentivise sufficient new production capacity to keep market for mined copper in balance over next decade. - Benchmark is to provide developers with ‘risk adjusted’ 12% IRR on pre-tax 100% equity basis (more on risk adjustment in next slide). - Cash-flow analysis of 113 projects show that an long term price of $3.50/lb will incentivise sufficient new mine projects to keep market in balance over next decade. - Increase from previous estimate of $3.00/lb primarily due to CAPEX escalation. - Risk on upside as large projects in lower part of curve such as Pebble and Resolution will struggle to be developed in this timeframe. - Some projects will come from ‘off-radar’ to replace these. - Requirement for explorers and project developers is to maintain pipe line of new projects in lower part of incentive price curve. - Technical and financial parameters are in many ways the easy part of the equation. Project developers must also address so called ‘soft issues; and also political and country risk…….. © Wood Mackenzie 12 **Delivering commercial insight** **www.woodmac.com** # **How do you quantify political risk?** ## **Wood Mackenzie risk rating criteria for countries with copper mine projects** Stable = no significant

© Wood Mackenzie 13 **Delivering commercial insight** **www.woodmac.com** # **How do you quantify political risk?** - One approach to risk adjusting the IRR required to incentivise a mining project is to reference to sove

reign fiscal risk ratings such as those estimated by the credit spread of an individual countries bonds with respect to US 10 Year Treasuries. However, this approach has little relevance to specific issues facing the mining industry. In this analysis we have quantified the risk by considering the history, the economy and the importance of mining for each country hosting major copper mine projects and dividing the countries into four groups as follows: 1. Stable countries where no risk adjustment is necessary. 2. Countries where the principle risk is that policies will change so that mining companies incur higher royalties, duties or taxes. 3. Countries where ownership restructuring in the principle risk. 4. The last category is countries having protectionist policies, blocking acquisitions by international and foreign companies or where projects may be expropriated or contracts re-assigned. A risk adjusted IRR is not relevant in these countries. (For projects located in countries in categories two and three we have ‘risk adjusted’ our baseline 12% IRR according to the expected impact of policy changes on net profits and the estimated probability of policy changes occurring). © Wood Mackenzie 14 **Delivering commercial insight** **www.woodmac.com** # **So where are greenfield projects getting developed?** ## **Greenfield projects (>20kt/a) in construction as of February 2013 or coming on line over previous 12 months** Canada Russia

Projects gaining approval are those where developers have undertaken long term engagement with local communities. - First contact between local communities and mining industry is at exploration stage. - Peruvian and Zambian governments have secured higher taxes/royalties, but this has not precluded project development. - Chinese mine development generally small scale. Statistics from China Non Ferrous Industry Association show ‘Fixed Asset Investment’ in copper mining and ore dressing capac

ity for through to November 2012 up 23% on equivalent period in 2011. - Low risk countries tend to be higher cost and permitting is more difficult. Mainly brownfield developments in USA (Pinto Valley Restart & Morenci expansion). Thompson Creek’s Mount Milligan project only addition over 20kt/a currently in construction in Canada. Sandfire Resources high grade DeGrussa mine only new capacity in Australia. © Wood Mackenzie 16 **Delivering commercial insight** **www.woodmac.com** # **What does the copper mine project pipeline look like?** Source Wood Mackenzie © Wood Mackenzie 17 **Delivering commercial insight** **www.woodmac.com** # **What does the copper mine project pipeline look like?** - Project incentive price (PIP) for more advanced projects generally around or below forecast LT price of $3.50/lb. - Relatively few projects at currently financing / board approval stage. Quellaveco (Anglo) and Mina Justa (Minsur) the two largest with a decision pending. - 63 out of 97 (65%) of projects shown are in countries where higher royalties, duties or taxes or ownership restructuring is the principle risk. - Projects located in countries ranked as ‘stable’ where no risk adjustment is necessary represent 8 out of 18 of those currently awaiting permitting. Out of those in construction, only 4 relatively small projects are in these countries. - Many more exploration stage projects than indicated. Wood Mackenzie tend to start tracking projects when some form of scoping study or preliminary production plan is available. © Wood Mackenzie 18 **Delivering commercial insight** **www.woodmac.com** # **Permitting – looking on the bright side!** ## **Impact of permitting issues** **Cost of infrastructure plus social and environmental costs** and environmental costs

Projects which made no economic sense a decade ago at $1.00/lb copper can now be reconsidered. - Increased taxes and roya

lties and the benefits of jobs created by the mining industry will only be realised if projects obtain necessary permitting and proceed (e.g. Greek government now fast tracking gold projects). - Permitting process in regions such as North America are time consuming. However best time to bring on a new project may be towards the end of the decade as the supply gap opens supporting copper price. - It is generally well known whether a particular site is environmentally or culturally sensitive. Allowing some pre-screening of where stretched exploration budgets could be spent. © Wood Mackenzie 20 **Delivering commercial insight** **www.woodmac.com** # **A structural surplus of copper is unlikely in the medium to long term** Returns to

© Wood Mackenzie 21 **Delivering commercial insight** **www.woodmac.com** # **A structural surplus of copper is unlikely in the medium to long term** - Challenges facing project developers as discussed in this presentation preclude undisciplined addition of production capacity. - Most copper mine production from primary producers. Uneconomic production won’t be supported by by-product revenue. - Large scale projects are required to realise the economies of scale needed to process lower grade ore. Only a limited number of companies can develop such projects and those companies don’t have the financial or human resources to develop multiple projects simultaneously. - Given high CAPEX requirements companies may prefer to buy production capability rather than develop organically. This doesn’t add to overall global mine production capacity. - Pressure from shareholders for returns may limit funds for exploration and project development. © Wood Mackenzie 22 **Delivering commercial insight** **www.woodmac.com** # **What does the global copper industry need from greenfield explorers?** ## **Summary** - Despite forecast surplus of mined copper over short to medium

term new production capacity will be required from 2017. 

- Requirement for projects that will provide their developers with adequate returns at a long term copper price of $3.50/lb and can obtain required permitting. 

- Constraints on project development mean that a structural surplus of copper is unlikely in the medium to long term providing support to long term price.
